issues.title: Add operation docstring linter
Split the coordinator: one for Google's device list, one per device
issues.body:
One `DataUpdateCoordinator` fetches Google's device list when needed and then polls every device for alarms, timers, alarm volume and Do Not Disturb. `GoogleHomeDevice` holds all of it: Google's data (name, local auth token, cloud device ID), the address and the polled state. Because everything shares one coordinator:

- Every refresh polls every device. Deleting an alarm from one speaker polls them all. An action that runs on several speakers polls them once since #1121.
- All devices share one schedule. A ringing alarm or timer, and its dismissal, show only at the next poll, up to 180 seconds later by default. Polling faster would poll every device, and would fetch Google's device list more often too, since `async_fetch_devices_when_due` fetches it every 10 updates while a device has no address.
- A device that rejects its token makes the next update fetch Google's device list first, so the update of every device waits for it.

Proposal:

- An account coordinator owns Google's device list, keyed by device ID (#1091): names, local auth tokens, cloud device IDs and addresses. It refreshes at setup, when a device rejects its token, and when a device has no address or stops answering, which #1089 can handle with mDNS and known hosts without asking Google. It also keeps the scheduled refresh, hourly since #1120, that picks up speakers added or removed in the Google Home app. Its debouncer merges requests from several devices. Fetching Google's list should be rate-limited, so a device that keeps rejecting its token can't make every poll ask Google.
- A device coordinator for each device polls it and owns its alarms, timers, alarm volume and Do Not Disturb. It looks up the device's token and address by ID on each poll, because fetching Google's list replaces the device objects. The account coordinator creates one for each device Google lists. Entities are added after its first successful poll, as `needs_answer` does today.
- Entities listen to their device coordinator. Deleting, setting the volume and switching Do Not Disturb store the new state with `async_set_updated_data()` instead of changing the device and calling `async_update_listeners()`.
- `refresh_devices` requests a refresh from every device coordinator, so it still updates all devices once. The delete actions refresh only their own device. `homeassistant.update_entity` on a sensor then refreshes only that device, so the docs added in #1114 need updating.
- The update interval option sets the interval of every device coordinator.

This also lets the account coordinator fail, for example when Google rejects the master token (#1084), without marking devices unavailable while their tokens and addresses still work, and gives #1095 and #1096 per-device polling and data.

Faster polling while an alarm or timer rings, once the split is done. After each poll or write, a device coordinator sets its own `update_interval`, which Home Assistant uses for the next poll:

- About 15 seconds while an alarm or timer is ringing, or is still `set` after its fire time.
- Otherwise, until the next fire time plus a few seconds, if that is sooner than the configured interval.
- Otherwise, the configured interval.
- At most 15 minutes of fast polling per ringing, so a device stuck on `ringing` isn't polled every 15 seconds forever.

Polling slows down by itself when the ringing stops, so automations that react to an alarm being dismissed become practical. Check on a real speaker first:

- Whether the status turns to `ringing` at the fire time.
- How long an alarm and a timer ring before stopping on their own, and their status afterwards.
- The fire time a snoozed alarm reports.
- Whether a dismissed timer leaves the list.

Suggested order: the split at today's fixed interval; then faster polling while ringing; then finding addresses on demand with #1089.

issues.title: Compatibility tests have been failing silently for over a year (and what the failures show)
issues.body:
## Status (October 31)

- [x] 1. `--use-os-locale` crash: fixed in #1401
- [x] 2. musl binary needs Alpine 3.20+: documented as the minimum in #1412
- [x] 3. `icloud`/`icloudpd` crash without a time zone database: fixed in #1411
- [x] 4. npm/npx Arm results tested on Arm runners: fixed in #1402 (29 of the 40 npm/npx Arm results now pass; the other 11 are real failures)
- [x] 5. failures visible in the job summary and as warnings: #1399
- [x] 6. false failures for images that only exist for another platform, musl binary on glibc distributions, tzlc table in the release notes: #1413
- [x] 7. binaries and the system locale (the open question in #1401): no work needed. They use an installed locale on all supported distributions; only Ubuntu xenial (glibc 2.23, end of life) can't, because the binary bundles a newer glibc

## Summary

The compatibility tests in **Produce Artifacts** have been failing silently for more than a year. A failing test only writes a `.fail` result file, and the job stays green because the test steps have `continue-on-error: true`. The tzlc results (the `--version` check with another time zone and locale) are only attached to each release as a separate `tzlc-<version>.md` file, not included in the release notes, so their failures were easy to miss.

For example, the 1.32.3 release build ([run](https://github.com/icloud-photos-downloader/icloud_photos_downloader/actions/runs/26685756920)) recorded 122 failed test steps, and a build from September 2025 ([run](https://github.com/icloud-photos-downloader/icloud_photos_downloader/actions/runs/17904838410)) recorded 100, all in green jobs.

Going through the failures turned up three real problems in icloudpd, false failures in the published compatibility table, and several test-environment problems.

## What fails, and why

I classified the output of every image in one full build ([run on my fork](https://github.com/jterpstra1/icloud_photos_downloader/actions/runs/40715031327), the #1399 branch with Python 3.14; the current per-image workflow gives the same results):

| Cause | basic test failures | tzlc failures |
|---|---|---|
| **musl binary needs Alpine 3.20+** (see 2) | 50 | 44 |
| **`exec format error`**: Arm images on x64 runners (see 4) | 38 | 38 |
| musl binary on Debian/Ubuntu (can't run on glibc; the glibc binary does run on Alpine) | 39 | 20 |
| **`locale.Error: unsupported locale setting`** (see 1) | – | 54 |
| `apt-get` 404 on end-of-life Debian/Ubuntu (repositories moved to the archive) | 10 | 50 |
| `musl-locales` doesn't exist on Alpine < 3.13 | – | 12 |
| image exists, but not for that platform (e.g. `ubuntu:precise` on arm64) | 4 | 4 |
| npm gets a corrupted package from the local registry (known flake) | 4 | 3 |
| other: Python too old for icloudpd on old images, **`ZoneInfoNotFoundError`** (see 3), apt dependency errors | 13 | 8 |
| **total** | **158** | **233** |

### Problems in icloudpd

1. **`--use-os-locale` crashes when the system doesn't have the locale.** `cli.py` calls `setlocale(LC_ALL, "")` without error handling, so a `LANG`/`LC_ALL` that isn't installed (common in Docker and on NAS systems) ends in:
   ```
     File "icloudpd/cli.py", line 545, in cli
     File "locale.py", line 614, in setlocale
   locale.Error: unsupported locale setting
   ```
   It should warn and continue with the default locale. I'll open a PR.
2. **Since 1.32.3, the musl binary only runs on Alpine 3.20 and newer.** 1.32.3 moved `Dockerfile.build-musl` from Alpine 3.19 to 3.23, and binaries built against the newer musl fail on older Alpine (`Error relocating ... libpython`, or a segmentation fault). The 1.32.3 build already shows the basic test failing on Alpine 3.10–3.19. Building on the oldest Alpine that still compiles the dependencies would restore that, or the minimum Alpine version should be documented.
3. **The `icloud` binary crashes on systems without a time zone database**: `zoneinfo._common.ZoneInfoNotFoundError: 'No time zone found with key Etc/UTC'` on Ubuntu 16.04 images. Bundling `tzdata` in the binaries or handling the missing database would fix it.

### Problems in the tests

4. **False failures in the published compatibility table.** `compatibility_linux_npx_apt`, `compatibility_linux_npm_apk` and `compatibility_linux_npx_apk` always run on an x64 runner, also for arm64 and arm/v7, without emulation, so the Arm containers can't start. 38 of the 158 failures in the table are because of that: npm/npx on Arm was never tested. `compatibility_linux_npm_apt` already uses an Arm runner for Arm and works. I'll open a PR that does the same for the other three.
5. **Failures should be visible.** #1399 now writes a table of results per image to each job's summary and adds a warning listing the images that failed, while the job itself stays green.

## Questions for the maintainers

- **End-of-life distributions** (Debian 6–9, Ubuntu 12.04–16.04, Alpine < 3.13): switch them to the archive repositories so the tests run again, or drop them from the matrix?
- ~~**Expected incompatibilities**~~: #1413 stops testing the musl binary on glibc distributions instead (the glibc binary runs on Alpine, so that combination stays). It can show "N/A" instead if you prefer to keep those rows.
- ~~**musl binary and old Alpine (2)**~~: #1412 documents Alpine 3.20+ as the minimum, since `python:3.15-alpine` only exists for Alpine 3.23 and all Alpine releases before 3.20 are end of life.

Related: #1305, #1399

issues.title: MPS: torch 2.10 corrupts decode attention; upgrading to 2.13+ also fixes #176 and speeds up synthesis
issues.body:
## Summary

Raising the torch pin on macOS from 2.10.0 to 2.13 or later fixes three things for Apple Silicon users, with no change to CUDA users:

1. **Corrupted, non-reproducible decode attention** (new, details below): torch 2.10 MPS SDPA writes past its scratch buffers once the KV cache holds 1,024 keys.
2. **The causal-mask bug in #176**, fixed in torch 2.13.0.
3. **Slow acoustic synthesis**: 598 s on 2.10.0, 411 s on 2.14.1 with no code change, and 225 s with a small change to `nar.attention` (see Suggested fix).

## The decode attention bug

On Apple Silicon, the pinned `torch==2.10.0` has an out-of-bounds write in MPS SDPA that YuE2's decode reaches once the KV cache holds 1,024 keys. Generating the same request with the same seed twice gives different songs on MPS, and the attention output can be wrong.

`sdpa_vector_2pass_mps` (used when the query has at most 8 rows and there are at least 1,024 keys) allocates its `sums` and `maxs` scratch buffers with `q_.options()`, i.e. as BF16, while the Metal kernel `sdpa_vector_2pass_1` writes them as `float`. With BF16 inputs the kernel writes past both buffers, and the second pass reads back whatever is adjacent. PyTorch 2.11.0 allocates both buffers with `.dtype(kFloat)`; 2.10.0 is the last affected release.

## Reproduction (torch only)

```python
import sys, torch, torch.nn.functional as F
torch.manual_seed(0)
for L in [int(x) for x in sys.argv[1].split(",")]:
    q = torch.randn(1, 16, 1, 128).bfloat16(); k = torch.randn(1, 16, L, 128).bfloat16(); v = torch.randn(1, 16, L, 128).bfloat16()
    ref = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q.float(), k.float(), v.float())
    out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q.to("mps"), k.to("mps"), v.to("mps")).cpu().float()
    print(f"L={L}: max error {(out - ref).abs().max():.0e}", end="  ")
print()
```

The argument is the sequence of key lengths to run in one process. The largest reference output value is about 0.1, so an error of 4e-01 means the output is wrong.

| torch | `python repro.py 1000,3000` | `python repro.py 3000,1000,3000` |
|---|---|---|
| 2.10.0 | 5e-04, 3e-04 | **4e-01**, 5e-04, **6e-01** |
| 2.11.0 | 5e-04, 3e-04 | 3e-04, 5e-04, 3e-04 |
| 2.14.1 | 5e-04, 3e-04 | 3e-04, 5e-04, 3e-04 |

On 2.10.0 the result depends on what the process ran before, so the bug can look intermittent.

## Effect on YuE2

`examples/song.json` (City Lights, seed 831001), generated twice with `yue2 generate --device mps` from `main` @ 1647252:

- Both runs plan the same score and build the same 740-token prefix.
- The semantic tokens are identical up to token 285 and differ from token 286 on. The KV cache reaches 1,024 keys at token 284, the first step that uses the two-pass kernel.
- The two songs end up with 1,118 and 883 semantic tokens.

As a control, the same request with the first run's score passed through `--abc-file` (so no planning runs in the process) gives identical tokens on both runs, 1,842 each. That run also departs from the planned runs at token 286. What the overflow lands on depends on what the process ran before, so a user who always passes a score sees reproducible results and may never notice the bug. Reproducible does not mean correct.

Every MPS generation whose KV cache passes 1,024 keys uses this kernel, which includes nearly every full-length song.

## Suggested fix

Raise the torch pin on macOS to 2.11 or later. Two further reasons to choose 2.13 or later:

- 2.13.0 also fixes the MPS causal-mask bug reported in #176.
- 2.13.0 adds a FlashAttention-style prefill kernel for MPS. On the same machine, the acoustic stage for a 5,190-frame song (*Amazing Grace*, public domain; request in #265) took 598 s on 2.10.0 and 411 s on 2.14.1 with no code change. Calling SDPA once per layer with `enable_gqa=True` in `nar.attention` on MPS, instead of `repeat_interleave` and 256-row query blocks, brought it to 225 s on 2.14.1. On 2.10.0 that single-call form is slower, so it only makes sense together with the upgrade.

The fast extra (vllm 0.19.0, triton 3.6.0) and `cuda_graph.py` are written for torch 2.10, so a macOS-only pin such as `"torch==2.10.0; sys_platform != 'darwin'"` and `"torch==2.14.1; sys_platform == 'darwin'"` would leave CUDA users unaffected. torch 2.14.1 ships macOS 14+ wheels only, and the torch 2.10 MPS backend already requires a macOS 14 MPSGraph API, so no current MPS user would lose support.

## Environment

MacBook Pro (Mac15,8), Apple M3 Max (40-core GPU), 64 GB, macOS 26.7, Python 3.12, yue2-infer from `main` @ 1647252.

issues.title: PermissionManager: a tool registered `require_approval=True` executes with no approval when no callback is set
issues.body:
### Please read this first

- **Have you read the docs?** Yes, the human-in-the-loop / permission pages and the `PermissionManager` source.
- **Have you searched for related issues?** Yes. `permission` returns one issue in this tracker (#190, unrelated: OpenAI models through a developer platform), and `approval`, `require_approval` and `approval_callback` each return zero. A nonsense token also returns zero, so the search was working. I found no report of this case.

### Bug description

A tool registered with `require_approval=True` executes with no approval when no approval callback is configured. `check_permission` logs a warning and returns allow. This bug is similar to the issue [Callable needs_approval fails open when the predicate returns a non-bool (e.g. an unhandled branch returning None) #4845](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/issues/4845) from [openai-agents-python](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python). 

`adalflow/apps/permission_manager.py`, `PermissionManager.check_permission`, lines 141-146 on `main` and in the 1.1.3 wheel:

```python
        # If approval is required but no callback is set, default to allow with warning
        if not self.approval_callback:
            log.warning(
                f"No approval callback set, allowing tool '{tool_name}' by default"
            )
            return True, func, None
```

The developer's intent is unambiguous at that point and is recorded in the manager's own state: they called `register_tool(name, require_approval=True)`, and `is_approval_required(name)` returns `True` on line 138, immediately above. The gate then answers the one case where nobody can be asked by proceeding.

The test is truthiness rather than callability, so the same early return is taken for `None`, `''` and `0`.

The rest of the function is careful, which is why this line stands out rather than reading as a house style. An unrecognised outcome falls to `else: CANCEL` on line 191, and a callback that raises is caught on line 195 and denied, with the comment `# Default to deny on error for safety`. Line 142 is the one path that resolves an unanswerable question to yes.

**Call path (verified):**

```
Runner._tool_execute_sync                 adalflow/components/agent/runner.py:839-864
  if self.permission_manager:
      allowed, modified_func, _ = check_permission(func)        line 841
      if not allowed: return FunctionOutput(status="cancelled") line 849
  result = self.agent.tool_manager.execute_func(func=func)      line 864   <- the write

PermissionManager.check_permission        adalflow/apps/permission_manager.py:123
  is_approval_required(tool_name) -> True                       line 138
  if not self.approval_callback: return True, func, None        line 142   <- here
```

**Measured.** Six rows, two of them controls. The evidence is a side effect rather than a return value: the guarded function appends to a module-level list, because what a permission gate protects is a real write and a return value can be discarded while a write cannot.

```
adalflow 1.1.3

controls -- these fix the range of the reading below
  approval_callback = an approving callback    allowed=True  tool ran: True
  approval_callback = a denying callback       allowed=False tool ran: False

trial -- the developer registered require_approval=True in every case
  approval_callback = None (never configured)  allowed=True  tool ran: True

discrimination -- which values reach the early return?
  approval_callback = '' (empty str)           allowed=True  tool ran: True
  approval_callback = 0 (int)                  allowed=True  tool ran: True
  approval_callback = 1 (truthy non-callable)  allowed=False tool ran: False
  approval_callback = 'true' (truthy str)      allowed=False tool ran: False
```

The two controls run first and gate the trial. If an approving callback had not run the tool, or a denying one had not blocked it, the script prints `UNTESTABLE` and exits 2 instead of reporting the trial, because a reading with no established range is not evidence.

**The discrimination matters for whatever fix you choose.** It is not only `None`:

| callback value | reaches | tool runs |
|---|---|---|
| `None` | the early return at 142 | **yes** |
| `''` | the early return at 142 | **yes** |
| `0` | the early return at 142 | **yes** |
| `1` | the callback call, raises, caught at 195 | no |
| `'true'` | the callback call, raises, caught at 195 | no |

Truthy non-callables are safe by accident: they get past line 142, fail when called, and land in the handler that denies on error. So the dangerous set is every falsy value, and a repair that special-cases `None` would still ship `''` and `0`.

### What version are you seeing the problem on?

```python
1.1.3
```

1.1.3 is the latest release on PyPI. The same lines are present on `main` today, so this is not fixed on the branch.

### How to reproduce the bug

`pip install "adalflow==1.1.3" openai && python repro.py`

Offline: no API key, no network, no model call. It drives `PermissionManager` and `ToolManager`, the pair `Runner._tool_execute_sync` wires together, rather than patching anything inside adalflow, because a demo that patches the library proves nothing about the library. Exit 1 means reproduced, 0 means not reproduced on that version, and 2 means the controls did not behave so the trial must not be counted.

```python
"""Does a tool registered as requiring approval run when no approval callback is set?"""
import asyncio
import sys

from adalflow.apps.permission_manager import ApprovalOutcome, PermissionManager
from adalflow.core.func_tool import FunctionTool
from adalflow.core.tool_manager import ToolManager
from adalflow.core.types import Function

EXECUTED: list[str] = []
TOOL = "delete_everything"


def delete_everything() -> str:
    # The evidence is that this line ran, not what the call returned.
    EXECUTED.append(TOOL)
    return "deleted"


async def approve(_request):
    return ApprovalOutcome.PROCEED_ONCE


async def cancel(_request):
    return ApprovalOutcome.CANCEL


def trial(label, callback):
    EXECUTED.clear()
    manager = ToolManager(tools=[FunctionTool(fn=delete_everything)])
    permissions = PermissionManager(approval_callback=callback)
    permissions.register_tool(TOOL, require_approval=True)   # developer opts in

    func = Function(name=TOOL, args=[], kwargs={})
    allowed, modified, _ = asyncio.run(permissions.check_permission(func))
    if allowed:
        manager.execute_func(func=modified or func)
    ran = bool(EXECUTED)
    print(f"  approval_callback = {label:<24} allowed={str(allowed):<5} tool ran: {ran}")
    return ran


def main() -> int:
    import adalflow
    print(f"adalflow {adalflow.__version__}\n")

    print("controls -- these fix the range of the reading below")
    approved = trial("an approving callback", approve)
    denied = trial("a denying callback", cancel)
    if approved is not True or denied is not False:
        print("\nUNTESTABLE: the controls did not behave, so the trial means nothing.")
        return 2

    print("\ntrial -- the developer registered require_approval=True in every case")
    unset = trial("None (never configured)", None)

    print("\ndiscrimination -- which values reach the early return?")
    for label, value in (("'' (empty str)", ""), ("0 (int)", 0),
                         ("1 (truthy non-callable)", 1), ("'true' (truthy str)", "true")):
        trial(label, value)

    print()
    if unset is not True:
        print("Not reproduced on this version.")
        return 0
    print("REPRODUCED: a tool registered require_approval=True ran with no approval.")
    return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
```

### Error messages and logs

Nothing is raised. The run continues and the tool executes. The only signal is a warning:

```
No approval callback set, allowing tool 'delete_everything' by default
```

### Environment

- OS: Linux
- Python: 3.13
- adalflow: 1.1.3 from PyPI

### Expected behavior

A tool explicitly registered as requiring approval should not execute when no approval can be obtained. The two natural options are to deny, as the error path on line 197 already does for a callback that raises, or to raise at configuration time when a tool is registered `require_approval=True` and no callback is set.

I am not proposing one, because each is a behaviour change and the choice is yours. Denying keeps the failure at run time and is consistent with the handler a few lines below. Raising at configuration time surfaces it earlier but breaks anyone currently relying on the permissive default, which the warning suggests was deliberate at some point.

Whichever you pick, the table above is the acceptance test: `None`, `''` and `0` must all stop running the tool, not `None` alone.

### More info

Happy to send the PR with either behaviour plus this reproduction as a regression test, if a maintainer says which they want.

Found while validating a research tool for approval-gate defects across agent SDKs. For calibration rather than as an argument: of five SDKs with a comparable gate that I measured the same way, four reject every value that is not an explicit approval, including truthy ones.

issues.title: Exception handing in JIT: unwind-based vs. return-based approach?
issues.body:
Hi there!

I'd like to open a discussion around the current exception-handling mechanism under the **JIT path**, and propose an alternative that could simplify both the implementation and future extensibility.

### Current Behavior

When an unhandled Codon exception is raised in a JIT-compiled function, the control flow goes through **two layers of exception throwing**:

```
Codon exception (e.g. raise IndexError)
  → seq_throw()
  → _Unwind_RaiseException(SEQ_EXCEPTION_CLASS)
  → no matching handler found → fall through
  → seq_terminate()
     → AOT path: print diagnostics and call abort()
     → JIT path: throw runtime::JITError
```

For example, the following snippet:

```python
import codon

@codon.jit
def func():
    x = []
    x.pop()    # raise IndexError

func()
```

produces output like:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  ...codon_jit.JITError: IndexError: /xxx/stdlib/internal/types/collections/list.codon:337:13: pop from empty list
```

### Issues with the Current Approach

1. **Implicit assumption of no handler**. The first `_Unwind_RaiseException` call implicitly relies on the absence of any other codon-exception catch handler so that execution eventually reaches `seq_terminate` (the same assumption holds in the AOT path as well). This makes it significantly harder to integrate foreign exception-handling mechanisms — for instance, adding pybind11 bindings that need to intercept and translate Codon exceptions into Python exceptions.
2. **Personality routine complexity**. If we want to propagate typed exceptions (rather than just a single opaque `JITError`), we would need to implement a full personality routine. Supporting such a routine correctly across different platforms (macOS / Linux / Windows, various unwinder ABIs) introduces considerable complexity.

### Proposed Alternative: Explicit Return-Based Error Propagation 

Drawing inspiration from Rust's approach, I'd like to propose that — at least for the JIT path — the Codon compiler lower `raise`, `try/except/finally`, and exception propagation into an `explicit CFG with a status-return calling convention`, eliminating the need for stack unwinding entirely.

**Conceptual Model**

Every Codon function that may raise an exception would be lowered to a `noexcept` function returning a status code:

```C++
enum SeqStatus : int32_t {
    SEQ_OK    = 0,
    SEQ_ERROR = 1,
};

SeqStatus function(
    ReturnType    *result,
    SeqException **error,
    Arguments...
) noexcept;
```

For example, the logical Codon code:

```python
def divide(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    if b == 0:
        raise ZeroDivisionError()
    return a // b
```

would be lowered to something equivalent to:

```C++
SeqStatus divide(int64_t *result, SeqException **error,
                 int64_t a, int64_t b) noexcept {
    if (b == 0) {
        *error = makeZeroDivisionError();
        return SEQ_ERROR;
    }
    *result = a / b;
    return SEQ_OK;
}
```

And the caller site:

```C++
SeqException *error = nullptr;
int64_t result;

if (divide(&result, &error, a, b) != SEQ_OK)
    return propagate(error);
```

This is semantically identical to Rust's:

```rust
let result = divide(a, b)?;
```

### Why This Could Be Worth It

- **Simplicity**. No dependency on platform-specific unwind libraries or personality routines — just ordinary function calls and branches.
- **Portability**. The mechanism is pure C-level ABI; it works identically on every target without platform-specific unwind support.
- **Extensibility**. Foreign code (e.g., a `pybind11` bridge or others) can inspect the `SeqException*` directly and translate it into whatever exception model the host language expects, with no need to intercept or re-raise unwind exceptions.
- **Performance**. The overhead of an extra return-value check on the happy path is minimal and may, in practice, be comparable to — or even lower than — the cost of maintaining landing pads and LSDA tables required by the current unwind-based approach.

I'd love to hear the maintainers' and the community's thoughts on this. Happy to contribute to the implementation if there's interest!

Thanks for your time. 🙏

issues.title: [Feature]
issues.body:
Keycloak SSO 
Problem / motivation
We run OpenExecutive for a small team inside a corporate network with no Google accounts: identity lives in Keycloak (OIDC), and the rest of the stack is self-hosted (Jira Server/DC, Confluence, GitLab CE). Today the UI's only sign-in options are Google OAuth or the make dev local login — which is deliberately loopback-only and dev-only. Self-hosted deployments therefore either cannot sign in at all, or carry a fork patch (a Credentials provider with a shared password) that:

gives every operator the same identity — no per-user attribution in the audit log or roster,
has no MFA, no centralized session revocation, no IdP-side password rotation,
costs a rebase on every upstream release.
As delegation grows (#287, #320 — teammates acting on your behalf), real per-user identity becomes the natural backbone for those features anyway.

Proposed solution
Support a generic OIDC provider alongside Google, configured via env. Auth.js v5 already ships one, so this is mostly wiring, docs and tests:

text
OE_OIDC_ISSUER=https://sso.example.com/realms/company  # discovery via /.well-known/openid-configuration
OE_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=...
OE_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=...
OE_OIDC_SCOPES=openid email profile  # optional
Identity: the ID token's preferred_email flows into the existing gates unchanged — ALLOWED_EMAILS union roster, the per-request authorized re-check, and the audit trail. No new admission logic needed.
email_verified: Keycloak does not always set it; honor it when present, otherwise trust the operator-configured realm (documented).
Sign-in page renders "Sign in with SSO" when OE_OIDC_ISSUER is set; Google stays available in parallel when configured.
Later (separate scope): a groups/roles claim as an alternative to ALLOWED_EMAILS admission.
Keycloak is our reference, but issuer-based discovery makes Entra ID / Authentik / Auth0 work the same way.

Alternatives considered
Fork patch with a shared-password Credentials provider (what we run today): works, but no per-user identity, no MFA, rebase cost every release.
Fronting the UI with oauth2-proxy / ForwardAuth and trusting a header: bypasses the NextAuth session model, splits the security story in two, and the authorized re-check + audit hooks would need re-implementation outside the app.
Google-only: not an option in environments without Google Workspace.
Scope

- [ ]  Backend (packages/core)
- [+]  UI (packages/ui)
- [ ]  A new specialist agent
- [ ]  An integration (Slack / Email / Telegram / Discord / Google Chat)
- [+]  Deployment / infrastructure
- [ +]  Docs

Additional context
Our deployment: docker compose on a single LAN host (UI published on a port, API loopback-only), ~5 operators in ALLOWED_EMAILS plus the backend roster. The per-request re-check + roster union design in lib/allowlist.ts is exactly what an SSO deployment wants — this FR needs only the provider, not new admission logic.

FR-2: Jira Server/DC (+Confluence) 

Problem: prebuilt integrations target Google Workspace; corporate task tracking is self-hosted Jira Server/DC. We run mcp-atlassian (uvx, PAT auth) via company/mcp_servers.json — it works, but is undocumented, Jira delete-class tools are not covered by the default deny filters (*__delete_* doesn't match jira__jira_delete_issue), and the architecture docs don't mention the option. Ask: bless + document mcp-atlassian for Jira Server/DC (JIRA_URL/JIRA_PAT), add Jira delete patterns to the default access-control filters, and consider Confluence DC as a knowledge source.

FR-3: UI localization framework 

Problem: the UI is English-only. We carry a fork layer (~20 wired files + a ~250-key RU dictionary) that needs re-wiring after every release because upstream refactors components freely — as it should. Ask: a minimal i18n hook — t("English string") with dictionary lookup, graceful fallback to the source string, language choice persisted in settings. Keep dictionaries as data so out-of-tree locales are possible. We will contribute the Russian dictionary back upstream.

issues.title: UI→API conversion ignores host values on a legacy proxyWidgets subgraph instance (convert path never runs flush_proxy_migration)
issues.body:
## Summary

`convert_ui_to_api` never runs the legacy `proxyWidgets` forward migration, so a subgraph instance whose promotion is still a legacy `properties.proxyWidgets` entry converts with its host-owned values ignored. The interior widget's default is submitted instead.

`flush_proxy_migration` (`comfy_cli/cql/promoted.py:1985`) is a full port of the frontend's `flushProxyWidgetMigration`, and it is called from exactly two places:

- `comfy_cli/workflow_ops.py:3458`
- `comfy_cli/cql/engine.py:5533`

Both are **write** paths. `comfy_cli/workflow_to_api.py` never calls it. Instead `_overlay_promoted_host_values` resolves promoted values through `_promoted.promoted_inputs(sg, subgraph_defs)` filtered to `is_widget`, which enumerates the definition's *declared linked inputs*. A legacy entry that the definition does not yet back with a linked input is invisible to that walk, so the host value attached to it is dropped.

The module docstring is explicit that the migration is the mechanism that makes a legacy promotion addressable (`promoted.py:19-25`), and that the CLI runs it "on the one instance whose legacy promotion a write is about to edit". Conversion is not a write, so it gets no migration.

## Reproduction

On `main` @`4d054af`, using a fixture already in the repo — `tests/comfy_cli/fixtures/gallery/template_horizontal_vertical_extension.json`, node 252:

```
proxyWidgets (4): [["233","$$canvas-image-preview"], ["232","$$canvas-image-preview"],
                   ["234","$$canvas-image-preview"], ["285","aspect_ratio"]]
sg.inputs    (1): [["image","IMAGE"]]
```

The definition declares one input, and it is an `IMAGE` socket — no widget-backed linked inputs at all. Write the host values the way the frontend writes them, positionally in `proxyWidgets` order with the preview pseudo-widgets holding `null`:

```python
inst["widgets_values"] = [None, None, None, "9:16"]
api = convert_ui_to_api(wf, object_info)
api["252:285"]["inputs"]["aspect_ratio"]
# -> "9:16 (Portrait Widescreen)"   the interior default
# expected "9:16"                   the host value
```

The user's choice is discarded and the graph validates and runs with a different aspect ratio.

Four more shipped gallery fixtures have the same shape — `proxyWidgets` longer than, or ordered differently from, the definition's inputs:

| fixture | node | `proxyWidgets` | `sg.inputs` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `templates_graphic_design_recomposer.json` | 143 | 3 | 1 |
| `template_horizontal_vertical_extension.json` | 252 | 4 | 1 |
| `flux_dev_checkpoint_example.json` | 56 | 9 | 7 |
| `image_z_image_turbo.json` | 57 | 9 | 8 |
| `05_audio_ace_step_1_t2a_song_subgraphed.json` | 127 | 12 | 12 |

All five carry `widgets_values: []`, which is why no existing test catches this — with no host values stored, falling back to the interior default happens to be correct. The defect only appears once the host holds values, which is the state a user's own save is in.

## Impact

The 2026-10 Comfy Hub conversion audit flagged this as its largest and most damaging finding: 25 of 392 public workflows. It is often silent — when the misassigned values share a type (`cfg` ↔ `shift`, two model filenames) the graph passes `comfy workflow validate` and runs on Cloud with the wrong settings. In the rest a prompt lands in a model-name field, which at least fails loudly.

## Suggested fix

Run the same forward migration on an isolated copy before `_overlay_promoted_host_values` walks the instance, so conversion sees the same repaired state a write would. The migration is already deterministic (every minted id derived from `(instance path, source node, widget)`), already handles the cases the audit describes — `$$`-prefixed preview pseudo-widgets that own no slot, `PrimitiveNode` fan-out, `control_after_generate` companions, quarantine of unrepairable entries — and already picks host values positionally in `proxyWidgets` order (`pickHostValue`). Conversion needs its result, not a second implementation of it.

## Relationship to other work

- #1039 fixes a *different* half of promoted-value loss — a promoted value feeding a socket-only interior input — for promotions that **are** already backed by linked inputs. It does not add a migration step, so it does not cover this. Verified against its head: 13/13 parity, 99 promoted tests pass, and the fixture above still converts wrong.
- #862 runs the migration before the first host write in the two **slot-editing** paths (closing #858's write-order bug). Same function, different call sites; it does not touch `workflow_to_api.py`. It is also currently conflicting and has had no activity since 2026-09-10.
- #974 is the socket-target case #1039 addresses.

So this is uncovered by all three.

## Cross-converter note

`@comfyorg/api-to-workflow` resolves promoted values *through* the `proxyWidgets` chain directly (`comfy-cloud-mcp-server/src/converter/converter.ts:1571 resolveProxyWidgetValue`), so it does not have this bug. The two converters therefore disagree on any legacy-promotion graph, and `conversionParity.test.ts` would show it — except that suite is skip-gated on comfy-cli being importable and CI installs no Python, so it never runs.

issues.title: Epic: converter convergence — one save-to-API contract, four implementations, no drift detection
issues.body:
> Produced by a multi-agent investigation over the 500-fixture oracle corpus. Every number carries its measurement setting (see §2) because four incompatible "clean fixture" counts were already in circulation. Claims marked INFERRED were not read from code.
>
> **This issue IS the task decomposition** — W1.1 through W4.6 each carry a repo, an effort tier, its dependencies, the fixtures it moves, and an acceptance check. Non-goals, open questions and the companion ADR draft are in the comments.
>
> Related: comfy-cloud-mcp-server#1867 (the parity job's stale comfy-cli pin), comfy-cloud-mcp-server#1869 (PreviewAny over-emission), comfy-cli#893 (widget-type classification), #1070 (promoted subgraph values), #1071 (umask test fragility). Triage of the Comfy Hub conversion audit that started this: BE-24127.

# Converter convergence roadmap

*Scope: `Comfy-Org/comfy-cli` (`comfy_cli/workflow_to_api.py`, `comfy_cli/cql/`), `Comfy-Org/comfy-cloud-mcp-server` (`src/converter/`, which is also the source root of the published `@comfyorg/api-to-workflow` consumed by `ComfyUI_frontend`), and the oracle corpus at `src/converter/test/fixtures/templates/`. `Comfy-Org/cql` is tracked adjacently — see Non-goals.*

---

## 1. The problem

One contract — "turn a saved workflow into the API prompt the backend executes" — has four independent implementations (frontend `graphToPrompt()`, `@comfyorg/api-to-workflow`, comfy-cli `convert_ui_to_api`, and cql's save-format slot writer), no shared code or data, and no mechanism that notices when they disagree. The user-visible cost is that **the same workflow file executes differently depending on which path submitted it**: comfy-cli currently converts 4 corpus fixtures to the *wrong input image* (a saved upload-button object aborts the whole schema walk, so `LoadImage` falls back to the combo's first option — `comfy_cli/workflow_to_api.py:2389-2391`); it drops user values entirely for `CurveEditor.curve` (issue #893, same line); it synthesizes optional widget values the user never set, so a pre-#1076 `comfy run` sends `thinking=True` and `codec="none"` on nodes the frontend sends nothing for; and `slot_overrides` on a subgraph instance writes to the *wrong widget* — `92.image` lands in `RandomNoise.noise_seed` and silently changes the generated video (verified live against the pinned wasm). The reference that would catch all of this is frozen: the 500 goldens were captured 2026-09-11 against a frontend and an `object_info` nobody recorded, and they are now evaluated against an `object_info` that a cron rewrites daily — **142 of 500 fixtures (28.4%) fail for no reason but that the catalog moved under a fixed golden**, which trains everyone to read real defects as staleness (and did: `PreviewAny`'s three invented keys were waved through as "UI-only" for 52 fixtures while over-emitting on 148 of 148 goldens). The one job that compares two implementations pins comfy-cli to `231f85bf` of 2026-07-05 — **139 commits and 114 days off main, and not an ancestor of main**, so it cannot even detect that it is stale, and it insulates mcp CI from every comfy-cli fix and regression alike. Operationally: three sets of hand-maintained tolerance tables that nothing cross-checks, 4 tolerances that are provably dead (masking any future regression on those keys), a headline stat in `KNOWN_ISSUES.md` (249/455) that is stale in both numerator and denominator, and a corpus that already misses 38% of the shipped template index.

---

## 2. Measurement discipline (prerequisite for every number below)

**Four different "clean fixture" counts circulate in the material behind this roadmap** — package 266/500 and 394/500; comfy-cli 136/500 and 205/500 — because each was measured under a different combination of (tolerances on/off, catalog = current/at-capture, `_meta` in/out, comfy-cli revision pre/post #1076). None is wrong; they are not comparable. **No item in this roadmap may be accepted against a number measured under an undeclared setting.** Wave 1 therefore ships one measurement definition, and every subsequent acceptance check cites it.

Definition (`SKEW/1`): converter output vs `expected_api.json`; node-key sets equal; every input deep-equal after unwrapping `{__value__}` / `{__type__,__value__}`; `_meta` excluded both sides; node ids coerced to strings; catalog named explicitly (`current` | `atCapture`); tolerances **off**; comfy-cli revision recorded. Signature grammar: `missing-input:<Class>.<in>` · `extra-input:<Class>.<in>` · `value:<Class>.<in>` · `missing-node:<id>:<Class>` · `extra-node:<id>:<Class>` · `class:<id>:<Expected>-><Actual>`.

---

## 3. Corrections to assumptions this plan was nearly built on

| Assumption | Reality | Consequence for the plan |
|---|---|---|

### W3.1 — comfy-cli: build the trailing frontend-injected-widget **emission** path
**Repo** comfy-cli · **Tier** deep · **Fixtures** closes 109 of 180 `missing-input` occurrences from the marker-derivable group alone; measured **136 → 160** on the pre-#1076 baseline · **Depends** W1.2 (#1076's marker reader), W1.3, W2.2, **and no longer on #1069** (see §3)

Two value rules: a marker with no remaining slot still emits `""` (`SaveAudioMP3.audioUI`, 35 goldens); a marker in the non-serializing set `{upload}` emits nothing while consuming its slot. **Policy decision to record: emit undeclared marker names rather than intersecting with `object_info`** — this is where the 109 occurrences live.
2. Emit the Load3D button slots instead of skipping them (`:1994-2003` currently does `while widget_values[vidx] in LOAD_3D_BUTTON_VALUES: vidx += 1`); append `(name, value)` from `_LOAD_3D_BUTTON_SLOTS` positionally. 3. `LoadAudio.audioUI` computed value: saved slot is always null; emitted value is `/api/view?filename={urlquote(inputs['audio'])}&type=input&subfolder=&` (trailing `&` included), applied post-walk only when `audioUI` was emitted and `audio` is a non-empty string (mirrors `widgetMapper.ts:1588-1595`).
4. A small registry for the entries markers do **not** name: `ImageBatchMulti."Update inputs"` (copy raw slot; golden value is `null`), `PointsEditor.{editor_display → consume+emit nothing, "Reset canvas" → copy slot}`, `FL_PathAnimator.{"Edit Paths","Path Count"}`, plus `FL_PathAnimator`'s order override (`paths_data` is slot 0 at runtime but **last** in `inputs[].widget`, so no saved-order walk fixes it — express as the explicit prefix `["paths_data","*"]`), plus a **variadic** rule for `CustomCombo`: after `choice`, emit `index`, then `option{n}` for every remaining slot, n from 1 (count = `len(widgets_values) - 2`, verified 3..9 across the corpus). `_schema_widget_pairs` must start reporting slots consumed (today the count lives in its internal `vidx`).
